Hello everyone,

my name is Daniel Soukup and I'm a master student at LMU Munich.
I recently started formalizing an Earley Parser in Lean for my thesis. My approach is to follow the work from Rau et Nipkow [1] - a verified Earley Parser in Isabelle -, but building it on top of the mathlib definitions on Context-Free Grammars.

I was wondering whether there is an interest for this kind of work and if (part of) it may be meaningful to contribute to CSLib? Reading CONTRIBUTING.md makes me think that the parser itself doesn't fit with the vision for reusable components and it would make more to sense to upstream extra definitions/lemmas about CFGs into mathlib currently?

[1] https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITP.2024.31

Daniel Soukup said:

Reading CONTRIBUTING.md makes me think that the parser itself doesn't fit with the vision for reusable components and it would make more to sense to upstream extra definitions/lemmas about CFGs into mathlib currently?

Hi Daniel! I think this is in scope for CSLib. We do want to have reusable components, but are probably less strict about this than Mathlib because of the nature of CS.

I see, that sounds reasonable. How would such a contribution look like preferably? Would I simply PR the finished work, so it's easier to tell whether its of interest, or would it be more sensible to PR some milestones of the project? For context, I am not using any AI, but this would be my first contribution and I'm already at around 1k LoC with the proved correctness of the model.

It's ideal for any PR , but especially a first contribution, to stay relatively small. It is also fine to open a PR with the full work so it's easier to see the big picture, then split off a series of self-contained smaller PRs on the order of a couple hundred lines.
You can split your work into small PRs but also provide a pointer to your personal repo containing the whole work, so that the reviewers of the small PRs know where you are going.

I'm teaching such material in my course, which I would like to port from English to Lean. I would be very interested to have a version of it or review it. It might be interesting to introduce first parse trees and then formulate a generic notion of a parsing algorithm that produces a parse tree or parse forest. This would indeed be reusable in that it could be used for CYK as a warm up and for incomplete parsers such as LR(1) in the style of Menhir ( https://gallium.inria.fr/~fpottier/menhir/ ).
